:::{#exm-sequence-limit}
#### A convergent sequence and a divergent one

- $a_n = \frac{1}{n}$ converges to $0$.
  Given $\epsilon > 0$, take $N$ to be any natural number larger than $\frac{1}{\epsilon}$.
  For every $n \ge N$, $\abs{\frac{1}{n} - 0} = \frac{1}{n} \le \frac{1}{N} < \epsilon$.
  For example, with $\epsilon = 0.01$, take $N = 101$:
  every $n \ge 101$ has $\frac{1}{n} \le \frac{1}{101} < 0.01$.
- $c_n = n$ diverges.
  For any real number $L$ and $\epsilon = 1$,
  every $n > L + 1$ has $\abs{n - L} > 1$,
  so no $N$ works.
  For example, with $L = 5$, every $n \ge 7$ has $\abs{n - 5} \ge 2$.
  It diverges to $\infty$:
  for every real number $M$, every $n \ge N$ has $c_n = n > M$
  when $N$ is a natural number larger than $M$.

:::
